analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The Fair Tax Act of 1999, which would have replaced every major federal tax with a 23% national sales tax, sat in the Ways and Means Committee and died without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill repeals the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes, and replaces them with a 23% national sales tax on nearly everything people buy [S2]. It abolishes the IRS as we know it and has state governments collect the federal sales tax for a small fee [S2]. Every registered household would get a monthly rebate covering the sales tax on spending up to the poverty line, and Social Security would be funded out of general revenue instead of dedicated payroll taxes [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and wealthy families gain the most in the long run: savings, investment returns, capital gains, and inheritances would never be taxed at all, and the estate tax disappears [S3]. Businesses would be freed from income tax compliance [S3]. Low-income households would be fully protected at the bottom by the monthly poverty-level rebate [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy households, savers, and family estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift taxes entirely [S2].
Gives every registered family a monthly rebate equal to the sales tax on spending up to the federal poverty level, so no household pays the tax on subsistence purchases [S3].
Ends income tax filing and compliance costs for individuals and businesses, and shifts collection to state tax agencies that already run sales taxes, paying them a 0.25% administration fee [S3].
Funds Social Security from general revenue after repealing payroll taxes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who consumes. A 23% tax 'of gross payments' means roughly a 30% markup on top of shelf prices, and because lower- and middle-income families spend nearly all their income while wealthier families save and invest, the burden falls disproportionately on working households once the rebate runs out. Retirees and savers who already paid income tax on their savings would be taxed again when they spend it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Working households paying tax on every purchase

drawbacks.text: The stated 23% rate is 'tax inclusive' — a share of the total price — so the real markup over today's prices is about 30%, and independent analysts have long disputed whether that rate could actually raise what the repealed taxes raised [S3].

Repealing payroll taxes and funding Social Security from the sales tax breaks the link between contributions and benefits, and makes old-age funding depend on consumption tax collections every year [S3].
The rebate requires annual registration with Social Security numbers for every family member, and families that miss the deadline lose months of payments [S3].
Repealing the estate and gift tax alongside the income tax means large fortunes pass untaxed while the tax base shifts entirely to consumption [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real simplification — no income tax filing, no IRS audits of individuals — and its poverty-level rebate genuinely protects the poorest households. But the structural trade is one-sided: it untaxes wealth accumulation forever while taxing every dollar of consumption, which shifts the burden toward households that spend what they earn. The transition alone — taxing again money that was already taxed as income — is a serious, well-known flaw. On balance the design favors households with large savings over households living paycheck to paycheck.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 106th Congress ended, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Linder introduced the Fair Tax Act of 1999 on July 14, 1999, joined by Rep. Collin Peterson, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day [S1].
The bill attracted 7 cosponsors — 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans — a fraction of the House [S4].
No further action was ever recorded: the Ways and Means Committee never scheduled a markup or a hearing, and the bill died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Essentially no one gained or lost — the existing income, payroll, and estate tax system simply stayed in place. The bill's sponsors got nothing, and households whose burden the bill would have raised were spared a change they never got to vote on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one — the tax system was left unchanged

for.name: Rep. John Linder
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal income, payroll, and estate taxes and replace them with a national sales tax [S1].

for.name: Rep. Collin Peterson
for.what_they_did: Joined Linder in introducing the bill, the only cosponsor named on the introduced text [S3].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — the only committee the bill reached
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup, hearing, or report was ever scheduled during the two-year Congress [S5].

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman through the 106th Congress, never brought the bill up for committee action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Support was small but genuinely bipartisan: 4 of the 7 cosponsors were Democrats and 3 were Republicans, with no votes ever taken to reveal a larger pattern.

industries.note: Repealing income, capital gains, and estate taxes means accumulated wealth is never taxed again, while the replacement tax falls on consumption — which lower- and middle-income families do at near-100% of income. The rebate softens but does not reverse that shift.
Abolishing the income tax eliminates the individual and business compliance market the industry depends on; its loss coincides with ordinary taxpayers no longer needing paid preparers.

The estate and gift tax repeal removes a tax on large transfers, and untaxed savings and investment flows would expand the asset-management base — though the bill taxes financial intermediation services under the sales tax.
States that keep their own sales tax become permanent collectors of the federal tax, keeping a 0.25% fee on everything they remit — a locked-in revenue stream and administrative role.

Sellers become the collection agents for a 23% federal tax — registration, segregated accounts, bonds for large sellers, and penalties for noncompliance — but receive a credit of the greater of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted.
